title: Secondary flow and particle focusing are read as trends against Dean number and radius, and a search that finds nothing is evidence only if the search was adequate
summary: One figure compares secondary-flow strength with two literature scalings across a Dean-number sweep, one records a feature the model did not produce, and one follows particles that migrate across streamlines in a pipe. Read each for its reference, its marked non-converged points, and what the footnote claims beyond the plotted data.

media.alt: Two log-log panels against Dean number from 2 to 260. Left: measured peak secondary-flow speed rising from about 7e-4 metres per second at De = 2 along a red dashed De-squared line, then bending below it and running above a purple dashed De-to-the-1.63 line; three red crosses at the highest De mark runs that did not converge. Right: the ratio of measured to a literature correlation, rising from 1.2 to about 2.5 near De = 20 and falling back to about 1.2, with a shaded band 1.2 to 2.5 and a green line at 1.

source.note: The figures carry PASS, FINDING and MISS labels and long footnotes. The page teaches the generic reading of a scaling-law check, a negative result and a particle-migration check with standard theory only, and quotes only numbers printed on the figures or computed from read-off points in the Apply script. The cfdcore project holds a near-identical set; this page does not repeat its walk-through.

read_the_figure.question: Does the secondary flow in a curved channel grow with Dean number the way theory says, does the model show the extra vortex pair the literature predicts at high De, and do particles in a pipe drift towards an intermediate radius from both sides?
read_the_figure.axes: Dean panels: x is Dean number De on a log axis from 2 to 260 (right panel) and on a log axis in the left panel; left y is the peak secondary-flow speed in m/s on a log axis, right y is the ratio of that speed to a literature correlation. Four-vortex panel: x is De on a linear axis from 0 to 260, y is the number of times a probe line crosses the outer wall region (0 to 4). Pinch panel: x is radial position r/R from axis (0) to wall (1); black dots are release radii, blue diamonds final radii after one pipe transit.
look_at: Left Dean panel: the blue line follows the red slope-2 line at low De, then falls below it; compare its slope with the purple slope-1.63 line, which is a slope reference, not the data.
Red crosses are runs that did not converge; they are shown, not dropped, and the line is drawn only through converged points.
Right Dean panel: the ratio is never 1. It climbs, peaks near De = 20 and falls; the ratio is the honest comparison because both curves span decades.
Four-vortex panel: the red line sits at 1 crossing for all 13 De values; the dotted line at 3 is the literature signature.
Pinch panel: inner particles move out, outer particles move in; none has reached either the model's equilibrium line or the literature line within one transit.
read_the_figure.proves: The Dean panels support the weak-curvature De-squared law at low De and show a regime change at higher De, with a quantitative gap to the literature correlation of 1.2 to 2.5 times. The four-vortex panel shows that one diagnostic never changed over the sweep. The pinch panel supports the direction of migration (a mechanism) but not the literature equilibrium radius.
if_wrong: A slope that stays at 2 over the whole sweep when the reference bends: the nonlinear coupling is not resolved, or unconverged runs were included as data.
A ratio panel that is flat at 1: the model and correlation are the same law, which would be suspicious for a different code path.
A vortex-pair signature present at one De but absent in a refined or continued run: the diagnostic is sensitive to resolution.
Particles all moving the same direction: the lateral force has the wrong sign or no balance.
must_check: The reference law, its source and its range of validity are named.
Unconverged points are marked and the fit range for each slope is stated.
A reference slope line is not mistaken for a reference value.
The quantity compared is the same in model and reference (here a ratio is plotted).
For a null result: the search method (continuation, perturbed restart) and its coverage are stated.
For migration: residence time or transit length is stated, since trend, not endpoint, is the evidence.
as_drawn: Left Dean panel: read-off points of about 6.7e-4 m/s at De = 2, 0.017 at De = 10, 0.06 at De = 20, 0.48 at De = 95 and 0.8 at De = 150. The label gives an exponent falling from 1.99 to 1.10 across the sweep. Crosses at De of about 190, 237 and 260.
Right Dean panel: ratio 1.2 at De = 2, about 2.5 at De = 20, about 1.27 at De = 150; shaded band 1.2x to 2.5x. The footnote says the speed stays within that band at all 10 converged points.
Four-vortex panel: crossing count 1 at De = 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 45, 63, 95, 127, 150, 190, 237, 260. Label: stayed at 1 crossing for De = 2 to 260.

Pinch panel: release radii about 0.1, 0.3 and 0.75 (two particles from 0.75); final radii about 0.19, 0.38, 0.645 and 0.695. Dashed lines at 0.5R (model) and 0.6R (literature). Label: mechanism confirmed, 0.5R versus 0.6R.

terms.meaning: Dimensionless group for flow in a curved channel: the Reynolds number times the square root of the curvature ratio. It sets the strength of the secondary flow.
Circulation in the cross-section of a curved channel, driven by the centrifugal force on the faster fluid in the core, superimposed on the main flow.
The slope of a log-log plot: y proportional to x to the power n has slope n, and a changing slope marks a change of regime.
Neutrally buoyant particles in pipe flow at moderate Reynolds number migrate across streamlines to an annulus about 0.6 of the radius from the axis (the figure's red line).
The use of that cross-stream migration, plus Dean flow in curved channels, to bring particles of a given size to a chosen position in a microchannel.
A nonlinear solve whose residual met its tolerance before the iteration cap; a point from a run that did not is a different kind of datum.
A diagnostic: how many times a chosen line through the cross-section crosses a sign change of a flow quantity. It is a proxy for the number of vortices, not the vortices themselves.

remember: On log-log axes the slope is the exponent; compare slopes with slope reference lines, and values with a ratio panel.
A dashed reference slope drawn through a data point says nothing about the level of the reference law.
Show unconverged points with a different marker and keep them out of the fit.
A mechanism check (direction of migration) and a quantitative check (equilibrium radius) are two different claims.
A null result is informative only to the extent that the search was shown to be adequate.

understand.title: Why the secondary flow grows as De squared at first
understand.text: The centrifugal force on the fluid scales with the square of the main-flow speed. For weak curvature the secondary flow is a small perturbation driven by that term, so its speed scales as De squared. At larger De the secondary flow carries momentum across the section and reshapes the main flow, so the growth slows: the local slope drops below 2.

understand.title: A slope reference versus a reference law
understand.text: The purple line has slope 1.63 and is anchored at the first data point. It shows what a power law of that exponent looks like. It is not the literature curve: the right panel shows the data lie 1.2 times above the correlation at De = 2, so a line through the first point cannot be the correlation. The ratio panel is where the level comparison is made.

understand.title: Direction versus equilibrium in migration
understand.text: Near the axis the net lateral force on a particle points outward, near the wall it points inward, so there is a radius where it changes sign. Particles from both sides head for it. Seeing arrows converge confirms that sign pattern; the position of the zero depends on the lift model, and the figure shows it lands at 0.5R where the literature value is 0.6R.

understand.title: What one null diagnostic can and cannot say
understand.text: A probe crossing count that stays at 1 says this diagnostic never changed. The footnote adds that another vortex-count quantity rises with De and is attributed to growing noise, and that a perturbed restart at one De relaxed back to the same state. That supports uniqueness at that De, but one restart at one De does not cover the 2 to 260 range, so the wording 'not an under-searched branch' goes beyond what is drawn.

steps.title: Dean number
steps.note: Re is the Reynolds number of the main flow, D_h the hydraulic diameter, R_c the radius of curvature. Curvature enters only through the square root.

steps.title: Local slope on a log-log plot
steps.note: Exponent between two points. Between De = 2 and 20 with speeds about 6.7e-4 and 0.06 m/s it is about 1.95.

steps.title: Weak-curvature scaling
steps.note: Dean's perturbation result, the red line. The figure's measured slope at low De is close to 2.

steps.title: Exponent of the correlation, from the ratio panel
steps.note: If the measured exponent is known and the ratio is plotted, the exponent of the reference follows by subtraction. Worked in Apply.

steps.title: Sign change of the lateral force
steps.note: The sign of the net lateral force flips at the equilibrium radius, so the migration is towards it from both sides. The figure's arrows have exactly this pattern.

steps.title: Probe count as a vortex proxy
steps.tex: N_\mathrm{cross}=\#\{\text{sign changes of }q\text{ along the probe}\}
steps.note: A count of sign changes of some quantity q along a line. A second vortex pair would add crossings; a smooth change of q without a sign change would not.

worked.title: The exponent of the literature correlation from the two panels
worked.problem: Read from the figure: measured peak speed about 6.7e-4 m/s at De = 2 and about 0.06 m/s at De = 20; the ratio of measured to correlation is about 1.2 at De = 2 and about 2.49 at De = 20. What exponent does the correlation have over this range, and is the purple line the correlation?

solution.text: The measured exponent between the two points.
Divide the measured values by the ratios to get the correlation values.

worked.answer: About 1.63, the exponent in the legend. So the correlation is a power law of that exponent, but it starts 1.2 times below the data at De = 2; the purple dashed line is anchored on the first data point, so it shows the exponent only and sits above the correlation. Read-off values carry a few percent uncertainty.

analyze.q: The ratio panel rises to about 2.5 near De = 20 and falls to about 1.2. If both curves were power laws with fixed exponents, what would the ratio look like, and what does the actual shape say about the measured exponent?
analyze.hint: A ratio of two power laws is a power law.

analyze.q: Three points are red crosses and the line stops at the last converged point. What would change in the reading of the high-De slope if they were included in the fit?
analyze.hint: Compare the crosses with the purple line.

analyze.q: In the pinch panel the particle that moves from 0.1 to 0.19 closes a smaller fraction of its gap to 0.5R than the one that moves from 0.3 to 0.38. What does that suggest about the lateral force across the section?
analyze.hint: Compute the fraction of the gap each one closes.

evaluate.q: The footnote reads the unchanged crossing count as a unique steady state. Which evidence supports that and which part of the claim goes beyond it?
evaluate.hint: One restart at one De versus a sweep over 2 to 260.

evaluate.q: The model equilibrium is 0.5R and the literature value is 0.6R. Is the mechanism validated, and is the quantity validated?
evaluate.hint: Direction versus value; none equilibrated in one transit.

create: Redraw the Dean panel so the reference law appears as a curve through its own values, the slope reference is visibly separate, the fit range is bracketed and the unconverged points are annotated with their De.

Design a continuation study from De = 2 to 260 that would make a null result on the vortex-pair transition convincing: starting states, step sizes, a diagnostic that would respond if the feature appeared, and the plot that summarises it.

checks.q: Why does the secondary-flow speed scale as De squared at small De?
checks.hint: Where does the driving come from?
checks.answer: The centrifugal force scales with the square of the main-flow speed, and for weak curvature the secondary flow is a small response to it.

checks.q: The speed rises from 0.017 m/s at De = 10 to 0.06 m/s at De = 20. What is the local exponent?
checks.answer: ln(3.53)/ln 2 = 1.82 (read-off values), a little below 2 as the slope starts to bend.

checks.q: Why plot the measured-to-correlation ratio in addition to the speed itself?
checks.hint: Two curves that span decades hide a factor of 2.
checks.answer: Over six decades of speed a factor of 2 is a thin gap on a log axis; the ratio makes it visible and shows it varies with De.

checks.q: A footnote says a perturbed restart returned to the same state at machine precision. How strong a claim is that?
checks.hint: Count the states tried and the De values covered.
checks.answer: It supports a unique state at the tested De. It does not cover the sweep, so it shows the search was not trivially empty but does not exclude a branch elsewhere.

checks.q: What would make a miss on a predicted transition into a positive statement about the model?
checks.hint: The search has to be adequate and the diagnostic sensitive.
checks.answer: A refinement study, continuation from several starting states, a diagnostic shown to respond to an imposed perturbation, and a stated limitation of the formulation if it still does not appear.

provenance.notes: Disclosure: the images carry PASS, FINDING and MISS banners, internal function and variable names (the footnotes name the peak-speed, probe-count, vortex-count and residual variables, a lift function, a lift-profile normalisation, and an iteration cap), an A.5/A.6 milestone prefix in titles, and a remark that fitted lift coefficients are 'paywalled' and a literature substitution was used. None are repeated on the page. Owner review: (1) footnote of the Dean figure says the slope declines toward the 1.63 asymptote at high De, but the plotted slope between De = 95 and 150 is about 1.1, below it. (2) The four-vortex footnote concludes a unique steady state, 'not an under-searched branch', from one perturbed restart at De = 150. (3) The same three figures exist in cfdcore; check the two pages are kept consistent. (4) The purple 1.63 line is anchored to the first data point and is easily mistaken for the literature curve.
